title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hookLine: life and death set before you: choose life
carry: the word is very near you

cards: The day after Ash Wednesday, when Catholics have just had ashes on their foreheads and heard remember you are dust, the Church opens the Bible to this page. Moses is near the end of his last speech.
He's given all the laws, the stories, the warnings. Now he does what a good teacher does at the end of a long course: he boils it down to one choice. Not a hundred rules.
Two roads. And in front of witnesses, he tells them which one to take.

teach.h: THE WORD IS VERY NEAR YOU.
teach.b: First, the nearness. Just before this, Moses says this commandment isn't too hard for you or far away. It isn't up in heaven, so that you'd need someone to go get it, and it isn't across the sea.
The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it. Second, the choice.

teach.h: LIFE AND DEATH, BLESSING AND CURSE.
teach.b: "I call heaven and earth to witness this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live."

Moses doesn't pretend there's no choice, and he doesn't make it for them. He lays both roads out plainly and then, like a parent, can't help saying which one he hopes they'll take. Third, what life means.
In Hebrew, the word for life, chayyim, is plural, as if life were never just one thing; the toast l'chaim, to life, comes from it.

And Moses says what that life is: loving the Lord, listening to his voice, holding fast to him, for he is your life and the length of your days. Choosing life, in Moses's words, isn't only staying alive.

Fourth, how Catholics carry it. Pope John Paul the Second drew on passages like this in his letter on the Gospel of Life, teaching that every human life, from its beginning to its natural end, is a gift to protect.
And the Church puts this reading at the start of Lent, a season of small choices, every one of them a road.

how: Deuteronomy 30:15–20 is read at Mass on the Thursday after Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, and Pope John Paul II's encyclical Evangelium Vitae (1995) draws on it in teaching the dignity of every human life.

games.q: you're Moses, at the end of your last speech. you've set life and death before the people. what's your final word?
o: choose life, that you and your children may live.
the choice is already made for you.
games.why: he can't help himself: choose therefore life. and he names what life is: loving the Lord, for he is your life.

practice: Look at the day ahead and find one small fork in it: bed on time or scrolling till two, calling your mother back or letting it go another week, the kind word or the sharp one.
See both roads clearly, the way Moses laid them out, and choose the one with more life in it. If you pray, ask for help to keep that choice; if not, commit to it quietly.

wordCard.voice: Choose life. Moses's final charge: life and death set before you, and a plea to choose life, and the God who is life. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall choose life. chayyim, life, is a plural word.

carryVoice: Your line: the word is very near you. Close enough to choose today. Day three hundred eighty-eight, in the books.
